lessons.title: Understand Basic Heating and Cooling Systems
lessons.why_this_matters: Customers may describe comfort problems without knowing their equipment type.

lesson_content.heading: Know the basics
lesson_content.text: Heating and cooling systems move or produce heat to control indoor comfort. Common systems include furnaces, heat pumps, air conditioners, and portable room units.

lesson_content.heading: Check before recommending
lesson_content.text: A thermostat controls temperature settings for compatible equipment. Air filters help capture particles in systems designed for them. Ventilation moves air between spaces or outdoors.

lesson_content.heading: Put it into practice
lesson_content.text: Product names do not establish system compatibility. Start by asking what equipment the customer owns and what task they are trying to complete.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer asks for a “heater filter.” Ask whether they have a furnace, heat pump air handler, or portable unit.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Do you know the equipment model, or can you show the filter label?”
common_mistakes: Assuming every heating system uses the same filter.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate unfamiliar equipment, combustion systems, or mechanical problems to a qualified technician.

optional_practice.question: Which detail best helps identify a replacement HVAC accessory?

choices.A: Equipment model and existing accessory label

optional_practice.explanation: Equipment and accessory labels help establish the correct category and compatibility.

lessons.title: Help Customers Select Air Filters
lessons.objective: Read filter size and performance information
lessons.why_this_matters: The wrong filter may not fit or suit the equipment.

lesson_content.heading: Know the basics
lesson_content.text: Filter labels often list a nominal size and an actual size. These can differ. Compare the existing filter markings and equipment instructions.

lesson_content.heading: Check before recommending
lesson_content.text: Filter performance may be described using MERV ratings. Higher numbers generally indicate greater particle capture under the rating method, but not every system can use every filter.

lesson_content.heading: Put it into practice
lesson_content.text: Airflow requirements matter. Do not claim that the highest-rated filter is always best. Check manufacturer guidance when performance or compatibility is unclear.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer wants the thickest, highest-rated filter available. Ask for the system’s recommended size and filter specifications first.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Let’s match the size and check what your equipment allows.”
common_mistakes: Choosing solely by MERV rating or nominal dimensions.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate airflow complaints or uncertainty about approved filters to HVAC support.

optional_practice.question: Why is the highest MERV rating not automatically the best choice?

choices.A: It is always the wrong size
choices.B: Equipment airflow requirements may limit suitable filters

optional_practice.explanation: Filter selection must consider the equipment’s airflow requirements.

lessons.title: Recognize Thermostat and Control Differences
lessons.why_this_matters: A thermostat that looks similar may not work with a particular system.

lesson_content.heading: Know the basics
lesson_content.text: Thermostats vary by supported equipment type, voltage, wiring, and features. Some systems use proprietary controls. A basic thermostat is not automatically compatible with a heat pump or multistage system.

lesson_content.heading: Check before recommending
lesson_content.text: Ask for the HVAC equipment model and the existing thermostat model. Manufacturer compatibility tools can help, but wiring questions belong to qualified support.

lesson_content.heading: Put it into practice
lesson_content.text: Never instruct a customer to connect unknown wires or bypass a safety control. Do not assume wire color alone identifies its function.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer wants a smart thermostat for a heat pump. Ask for model details and point them to the manufacturer’s compatibility process.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “We need to confirm your system and wiring requirements before recommending a thermostat.”
common_mistakes: Claiming compatibility based on thermostat appearance.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate unknown wiring, line-voltage controls, and system modifications.

optional_practice.explanation: Wire colors are not a reliable substitute for verified wiring information.

lessons.title: Compare Portable Comfort Products
lessons.why_this_matters: Portable heaters and fans have different limitations and hazards.

lesson_content.heading: Know the basics
lesson_content.text: Fans move air but do not necessarily lower the room’s air temperature. Portable air conditioners require appropriate venting and electrical supply. Dehumidifiers remove moisture from air.

lesson_content.heading: Check before recommending
lesson_content.text: Portable heaters require careful attention to manufacturer clearances, electrical ratings, and use restrictions. They should not be recommended with extension cords or power strips unless the manufacturer explicitly permits the setup.

lesson_content.heading: Put it into practice
lesson_content.text: Ask about room size, moisture, outlet availability, and intended location. Do not promise a particular temperature change without verified product data.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer wants a space heater for a small workshop. Discuss the listed room application and safety clearances, then review the manufacturer instructions.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Ask: “Where will you use it, and what does the product label say about the space and power supply?”
common_mistakes: Recommending a heater based only on advertised wattage.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate unsafe wiring, fuel-burning heaters, or unusual installation needs.

lessons.title: Recognize HVAC Warning Signs
lessons.why_this_matters: Some comfort complaints indicate safety issues, not accessory needs.

lesson_content.heading: Know the basics
lesson_content.text: Gas odors, carbon monoxide alarm activation, suspected refrigerant leaks, and electrical burning smells are not routine retail troubleshooting questions.

lesson_content.heading: Check before recommending
lesson_content.text: Carbon monoxide is a dangerous gas that people cannot reliably detect by smell. A CO alarm requires following emergency guidance and contacting appropriate responders. Never suggest ignoring or disabling an alarm.

lesson_content.heading: Put it into practice
lesson_content.text: Employees can identify packaged accessories and explain labels. They should not diagnose combustion equipment, handle refrigerants, or coach unsafe repairs.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer says a carbon monoxide alarm sounded near a gas furnace. Do not recommend a new filter as the solution.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Follow the alarm’s emergency instructions and contact emergency services or the appropriate utility or qualified professional.”
common_mistakes: Treating a CO alarm as a minor equipment nuisance.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate gas, CO, refrigerant, combustion, and serious electrical concerns immediately.

optional_practice.question: A customer reports a carbon monoxide alarm. What should you recommend?

choices.A: Ignore it if the house feels warm
choices.B: Follow emergency guidance and seek appropriate help

optional_practice.explanation: A CO alarm is a safety warning requiring appropriate emergency action.
